editorialPolicy.storyFidelity: The twelve sessions preserve the complete original 36-chapter arc, causal sequence, major choices, consequences, reunions, and ending.
editorialPolicy.foundation: Concrete, speakable sentences with one main action and mostly 6–11 words per line.
editorialPolicy.core: Connected sentences with cause, contrast, and reaction, mostly 10–18 words per line.
editorialPolicy.studio: Literary but performable sentences that preserve narrator wit, suspense, and moral tension.
editorialPolicy.safety: Historic peril and slapstick retain their narrative consequence without added graphic detail.
editorialPolicy.narration: Generate one continuous master per session and level; Watch and Mimic must seek within the same performance.
editorialPolicy.classTime: The story text remains concise; sixty minutes comes from deliberate replay, recording, comparison, retrieval, and sentence reconstruction—not padding the narration.

narration.direction: Begin physically exhausted, let the Tunny rescue feel grateful, move through daily labor with steady warmth, and make the transformation quiet, earned, and emotionally complete.
narration.productionRule: Generate one continuous master per session and level; Watch and Mimic seek within that exact same master.

livingStorybook.artBrief: A dawn-to-morning transformation stage links the Tunny rescue, poor Fox and Cat, Cricket's straw cottage, well and milk, Lamp-Wick's stable, basket work and study lamp, Snail's news, Fairy dream, renewed home, and old marionette by the chair.

beats.summaryKo: 힘이 다한 부자를 Tunny가 해변으로 옮긴다.
Fox와 Cat의 몰락을 보고 다시 속지 않는다.
매일 백 번 물을 길어 제페토를 돌본다.
장난감 나라의 친구가 치른 대가를 마주한다.
자신의 옷값을 아픈 Fairy에게 모두 보낸다.
이미 달라진 마음이 마침내 새로운 몸으로 나타난다.

lines.text: Pinocchio carried Geppetto until his strength disappeared.
The friendly Tunny carried them safely ashore.
The poor Fox and Cat begged beside the road.
Pinocchio remembered their theft and walked past them.
The Talking Cricket welcomed them into a cottage.
Pinocchio apologized and made Geppetto a bed.
Farmer John offered milk for one hundred buckets.
Pinocchio worked daily to feed his weak father.
He found Lamp-Wick dying as a tired donkey.
For five months, Pinocchio worked and studied.
He made baskets and built Geppetto a chair.
He saved fifty pennies for new clothes.
Then the Snail said the Fairy was sick.
Pinocchio gave her everything and worked twice as hard.
The Fairy rewarded his loving heart in a dream.
He woke as a real boy beside a healthy Geppetto.

lines.text: Pinocchio carried Geppetto through the sea until his strength began failing.
The friendly Tunny arrived and carried both exhausted travelers safely ashore.
On the road, the ruined Fox and Cat begged their former victim for money.
Pinocchio remembered their theft, rejected their excuses, and continued with his father.
The Talking Cricket welcomed them into a small straw cottage.
Pinocchio apologized for the hammer and prepared a bed for Geppetto.
Farmer John offered warm milk in exchange for one hundred buckets of water.
Every morning, Pinocchio completed the hard work to feed his weak father.
At the farm, he discovered Lamp-Wick dying after a donkey's life of exhaustion.
For five months, Pinocchio worked by day and studied by lamplight.
He sold baskets, supported Geppetto, and built him a comfortable rolling chair.
Eventually he saved fifty pennies and planned to buy new clothes.
The Snail then reported that the Blue Fairy was sick and penniless.
Pinocchio gave away every coin and doubled his work for her.
That night, the Fairy praised his loving heart and forgave his past.
He awoke as a real boy in a renewed home beside a healthy Geppetto.

lines.text: Pinocchio carried Geppetto toward the distant shore until exhaustion finally overcame his wooden strength.
The Tunny, inspired by their escape, arrived at the critical moment and carried father and son to safety.
Along the road, the ruined Fox and Cat begged from the victim whose trust they had once converted into profit.
Pinocchio recognized the consequence of their old deception, rejected their excuses, and calmly continued onward.
The Talking Cricket offered shelter in a straw cottage and reminded Pinocchio of the hammer thrown long ago.
Instead of defending himself, Pinocchio apologized, accepted the rebuke, and prepared a bed for his weakened father.
Farmer John offered one glass of milk in exchange for the exhausting labor of drawing one hundred buckets.
Every dawn Pinocchio returned to the well, transforming work into food and care for Geppetto.
In the stable he found Lamp-Wick dying as an overworked donkey, the final human cost of Toyland's promise.
For five months Pinocchio made baskets, studied by lamplight, and built a rolling chair for his recovering father.
His daily habits produced enough security for Geppetto and fifty saved pennies for a long-delayed new suit.
Before he could spend them, the Snail reported that the Blue Fairy lay ill without money for food.
Pinocchio surrendered every penny and chose to double his labor for the mother who had repeatedly rescued him.
That night the Fairy appeared in a dream, praising not perfection but the loving heart revealed through action.
He awoke in a renewed home as a living boy, while Geppetto stood healthy and young beside his workbench.
Looking at the abandoned wooden body, Pinocchio understood that becoming human had happened before his appearance changed.
